# 1- Getting and preparing the data and EDA

```{r}
df = data.table::fread("telematics_syn-032021.csv")

# quick cleaning process 
colSums(is.na(df))
table(df$Insured.sex, df$Marital)
table(df$Car.use, df$Region)
summary(df)

# replacing weird values 
length(df[df$Car.age <0, ]) # 52 
#replace by the median car age 
median_age <- median(df$Car.age[df$Car.age >= 0], na.rm = TRUE)
df$Car.age[df$Car.age < 0] <- median_age

# distribution of claims in the portfolio 
table(df$NB_Claim) # there is clearly a class imbalance, most of the contract have zero claims 

```
- no missing values; only two sex (male and female); Two factors in Regions (urban and rural)
- 4 factors in car use : commercial, commute, farmer, private 
- no abnormal
- Policy holders age go from 16 to 103 with a median age of 51
- there is a negative car age, that is some of the car age are < 0, how many? 52 lines, theses are mistakes ? so replace them by the median age 
- NB claim has a max of 3, meaning that no contract has over 3 claims and the minimum is zero , since that is the class we are trying to predict

| **Block**                     | **Columns**                                                                                                              | **Notes**                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Contract / exposure**       | Duration                                                                                                                 | In **DAYS**. Divide by 365 to get the exposure in years used as the log-offset.                                                                             |
| **Traditional (10)**          | Insured.age, Insured.sex, Car.age, Marital, Car.use, Credit.score, Region, Annual.miles.drive, Years.noclaims, Territory | Classic underwriting rating factors. Territory has many levels (\~55), which is a known problem for GLMs.                                                   |
| **Telematics – intensity**    | Annual.pct.driven, Total.miles.driven, Avgdays.week                                                                      | Usage volume.                                                                                                                                               |
| **Telematics – day mix**      | Pct.drive.mon, ..., Pct.drive.sun, Pct.drive.wkday, Pct.drive.wkend                                                      | Compositional variables: these sum to approximately 1 by construction. Do not include all of them in a GLM simultaneously.                                  |
| **Telematics – time mix**     | Pct.drive.2hrs, Pct.drive.3hrs, Pct.drive.4hrs, Pct.drive.rush am, Pct.drive.rush pm                                     | Trip length and rush-hour exposure.                                                                                                                         |
| **Telematics – harsh events** | Accel.06/08/09/11/12/14miles, Brake.06/08/09/11/12/14miles                                                               | Counts per unit distance above increasing g-force thresholds. Monotone nested structure: the 06-threshold count ≥ the 14-threshold count. Highly collinear. |
| **Telematics – cornering**    | Left.turn.intensity08–12, Right.turn.intensity08–12                                                                      | Same nested-threshold structure.                                                                                                                            |
| **Response**                  | NB\_Claim, AMT\_Claim                                                                                                    | Claim count and aggregate claim amount. **NB\_Claim** is the target variable.                                                                               |

## distribution of claims 

- Cameron - Trivedi Score test : A formal test of H₀: Var = μ against 
H₁: Var = μ + αμ² (the NB2 variance function). Construct the auxiliary variable and test whether its mean is zero:
```{r}

# checking if it follows a poisson or negative binomial (overdispersion)
var(df$NB_Claim)/mean(df$NB_Claim) # greter than 1 so overdispersion ? 
# a statistcall check Cameron–Trivedi score test

m_pois <- glm(
  NB_Claim ~ Insured.age + Credit.score,
  offset = log(Exposure),
  family = poisson(),
  data = df
)

dispersiontest(m_pois) # p value > 0.01 so we reject the posson distribution 

```

## actuarial analysis of claims 
### for continuous variables 
```{r}
freq_band_plot <- function(dt,
                           var,
                           exposure = "Exposure",
                           target = "NB_Claim") {

  dt <- as.data.table(dt)

  # Aggregate by variable
  res <- dt[
    ,
    .(
      Exposure = sum(get(exposure), na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims   = sum(get(target), na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    by = var
  ]

  # Frequency
  res[, Frequency := Claims / Exposure]

  # Scaling factor for dual axis
  scale_factor <- max(res$Exposure, na.rm = TRUE) /
                  max(res$Frequency, na.rm = TRUE)

  p <- ggplot(
    res,
    aes_string(x = var)
  ) +
    geom_col(
      aes(y = Exposure),
      fill = "lightblue",
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    geom_line(
      aes(y = Frequency * scale_factor, group = 1),
      color = "red",
      linewidth = 1.2
    ) +
    geom_point(
      aes(y = Frequency * scale_factor),
      color = "red",
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Exposure",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        ~ . / scale_factor,
        name = "Claim Frequency"
      )
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Claim Frequency by", var),
      x = var
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
    )

  print(p)

  return(res)
}

```
## for categorical variables 
```{r}

freq_cat_plot <- function(dt,
                          var,
                          exposure = "Exposure",
                          target = "NB_Claim") {

  # Aggregate by category
  res <- dt[
    ,
    .(
      Exposure = sum(get(exposure), na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims = sum(get(target), na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    by = var
  ]

  # Rename category column
  setnames(res, var, "Category")

  # Observed frequency
  res[, Frequency := Claims / Exposure]

  # Sort by frequency for easier interpretation
  setorder(res, Frequency)

  # Scale factor for dual axis
  scale_factor <- max(res$Exposure, na.rm = TRUE) /
                  max(res$Frequency, na.rm = TRUE)

  p <- ggplot(res,
              aes(x = reorder(Category, Frequency))) +
    geom_col(
      aes(y = Exposure),
      fill = "lightblue",
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    geom_line(
      aes(y = Frequency * scale_factor, group = 1),
      color = "red",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      aes(y = Frequency * scale_factor),
      color = "red",
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Exposure",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        ~ . / scale_factor,
        name = "Observed Frequency"
      )
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Observed Frequency by", var),
      x = var
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
    )

  print(p)

  return(res)
}
```

## modifications to continuous variables 
we will create age bands for the insurer age using frequency patterns 
Band	Age Range	Rationale
- **Young Drivers**	18–25	Very high frequency (peaks at ~20–23)
- **Early Career**	26–35	Elevated but declining frequency
- **Established**	36–50	Moderate, stable frequency
- **Mature**	51–65	Lower, stable frequency
- **Senior**	66+	Very low frequency (sparse data)

### Years no claims 
we observe a non linear relationship, so we need to create bands , then check if the bands 
created represent the actual correct relationship 

```{r}
dt[, NCDBand := cut(Years.noclaims, 
                    breaks = c(-Inf, 2,4, 9 , 19, 34, Inf), 
                    labels = c("0-2",  "3-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-34", "35+"))]

  res2 <- dt[
    ,
    .(
      exposure = sum(Exposure),
      Claims = sum(NB_Claim)
    ),
    by = NCDBand
  ][order(NCDBand)]
# check using negative binomial glm 
  m_line = glm.nb(NB_Claim ~ Years.noclaims + offset (log(Exposure)), dt)
  m_band = glm.nb(NB_Claim ~ NCDBand  + offset (log(Exposure)), dt)
  m_spline = glm.nb(NB_Claim ~ splines::ns(Years.noclaims, 4) + offset (log(Exposure)), dt)
  
AIC(m_line, m_band, m_spline)

```
clearly approximating the effect of Years.no.claims by a spline is far better, lets tune the hyperparameter that is the degree of fredom ( **dont use**)
```{r}
sapply(2:7, function(k) AIC(glm(NB_Claim ~ splines::ns(Years.noclaims, k) + offset (log(Exposure)), dt, family = poisson))
  ) # keep 4 as df 

# testing the accuyracy on the zero exposure region of years.noclaims *
tail(dt[
    ,
    .(
      exposure = sum(Exposure),
      Claims = sum(NB_Claim)
    ),
    by = Years.noclaims 
  ][order(Years.noclaims)], 25)
# candidates cap + no caps 
caps = c(25, 30, 35, 40, 45, Inf )
res_cap = data.table::rbindlist(lapply(caps, function(cp){
  # d = data.table :: copy(dt)
 NCD = pmin(dt$Years.noclaims, cp)
  m = glm(NB_Claim ~ splines::ns(NCD, 4) + offset (log(Exposure)), dt, family = poisson)
  data.table(cap =cp, AIC = AIC(m))
}
  
  ))

res_cap[order(AIC)]
```

# modifications of the categorical columns 
- Car.use : Most of the exposure is observed in the Private and Commute segments, while the Farmer and Commercial segments account for only a small proportion of the portfolio. Given the low exposure and the potential volatility of observed claim frequencies in these categories, Farmer and Commercial will be grouped with the larger categories to ensure more reliable risk estimation.

```{r}

     fifelse(Car.use == "Farmer", "Private",
     fifelse(Car.use == "Commercial", "Commute",Car.use ))]
```

# 2. VARIABLES SELECTION 

## 2.1 splitting 
Split 60 / 20 / 20 into training, validation and testing, stratified on whether a claim occurred so that the rare positive class is represented in all three. Because this dataset is cross-sectional, a simple random split is valid 
```{r}

set.seed(123)
df  = as.data.frame(dt)
# mutate the categorical to factors 
df <- df %>%
  rename(
    Pct.drive.rush.pm = `Pct.drive.rush pm`,
    Pct.drive.rush.am = `Pct.drive.rush am`
  ) %>%
  mutate( # here i am creatiung new variable (factors that i will add into a new model)

    Car.age.band = case_when(
      Car.age <= 2                  ~ "0-2",
      Car.age <= 5                  ~ "3-5",
      Car.age <= 10                 ~ "5-10",
      TRUE                          ~ "10+"
    ),

    Credit.score.band = case_when(
      Credit.score < 600            ~ "<600",
      Credit.score < 700            ~ "600-700",
      Credit.score < 850            ~ "700-850",
      TRUE                          ~ "850+"
    ),
    Insured.age.band = cut(
      Insured.age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 20, 30, 40, 60, Inf),
      labels = c("≤20", "21-30", "31-40", "41-60", "60+"),
      right = TRUE
    )
    ,

    Years.noclaims.band = case_when(
      Years.noclaims <= 5           ~ "0-5",
      Years.noclaims <= 10          ~ "5-10",
      Years.noclaims <= 20          ~ "10-20",
      Years.noclaims <= 30          ~ "20-30",
      TRUE                          ~ "30+"
    )
  ) 

df = df %>%  mutate(
    across(
      c(Insured.sex, Marital, Region, 
        Car.use, Car.use.grp, Years.noclaims.band, Credit.score.band, Insured.age.band,
        Car.age.band),
      factor
    )
  )
df$HasClaim <- ifelse(df$NB_Claim > 0, 1, 0)
# 60% train
train_idx <- createDataPartition(df$HasClaim,
                                 p = 0.60,
                                 list = FALSE)

train <- df[train_idx, ]
temp  <- df[-train_idx, ]
# Split remaining 40% into 20/20
valid_idx <- createDataPartition(temp$HasClaim,
                                 p = 0.50,
                                 list = FALSE)

valid <- temp[valid_idx, ]
test  <- temp[-valid_idx, ]

# Variables to use
Telematrics_vars = c("Total.miles.driven", "Pct.drive.rush.pm", "Pct.drive.rush.am",
                     "Pct.drive.wkend","Avgdays.week", "Brake.14miles", "Right.turn.intensity12",
                     "Left.turn.intensity12", "Accel.14miles")
features <- setdiff(
  c(
    continuous_var,
    categorical_var,
    Telematrics_vars,
    "Car.use.grp",
    "Exposure", "Years.noclaims.band", "Credit.score.band", "Insured.age.band","Car.age.band"
  ),
  c("Accel.14miles", "Car.use")
)

# X datasets
X_train <- train %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(features))

X_valid <- valid %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(features))

X_test <- test %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(features))

# y datasets
y_train <- train$NB_Claim
y_valid <- valid$NB_Claim
y_test  <- test$NB_Claim
# define formula for the glm 
formula_glm <- NB_Claim ~
  ns(Car.age, df = 4) +
  ns(Credit.score, df = 4) +
  ns(Years.noclaims, df = 4) +
  Insured.age +
  Insured.sex +
  Marital +
  Region +
  Car.use.grp +
  Total.miles.driven +
  Pct.drive.rush.pm +
  Pct.drive.rush.am +
  Pct.drive.wkend +
  Avgdays.week +
  Brake.14miles +
  Right.turn.intensity12 +
  Left.turn.intensity12 +
  offset(log(Exposure))
## First varibale selections using VIF to remove highly collinear variables 
train_glm <- cbind(
  NB_Claim = y_train,
  X_train
) # temp traing full dataset 
test_glm <- cbind(
  NB_Claim = y_test,
  X_test
) # test daastet 

valid_glm <- cbind(
  NB_Claim = y_valid,
  X_valid
)
m_full <- glm.nb(
  formula = formula_glm,
  data = train_glm
)
car::vif(m_full)
################################# SECONDE SELECTION stepwise regression + ANOVA 

# Modèle complet (M_1)
M_1 <- glm.nb(formula = formula_glm,
  data = train_glm)
# Modèle réduit sans variable (M_0)
M_0 <- glm.nb(NB_Claim ~ 1, data = train_glm)

# Sélection stepwise basée sur AIC
model_aic1 <- stats :: step(M_0, 
                                scope = list(lower = M_0, upper = M_1),
                                direction = "both",
                                trace = 0)
summary(model_aic1)
# check if some of the variables should be dropped 
drop1(model_aic1, test = "Chisq")

# i will drop 
- Avgdays.week ; 
model_aic1 <- update(
  model_aic1,
  . ~ . - Avgdays.week 
)
drop1(model_aic1, test = "Chisq")
pseudo_r_1 = pR2(model_aic1)["McFadden"] 

# look at the ways the splines look 
ggpredict(model_aic1, terms = "Years.noclaims") |>
plot()
ggpredict(model_aic1, terms = "Car.age") |>
plot()
ggpredict(model_aic1, terms = "Credit.score") |>
plot()
# ggpredict(model_aic1, terms = "Insured.age") |>
# plot()

# having observed these graphs, we are going to create new bands for some of the variables 
#and integrate them into the dataset then build an new model and compare the AIC 
formula_glm2 <- NB_Claim ~
  Car.age.band +
  Credit.score.band +
  Years.noclaims.band +
  Insured.age.band +
  Insured.sex +
  Marital +
  Region +
  Car.use.grp +
  Total.miles.driven +
  Pct.drive.rush.pm +
  Pct.drive.rush.am +
  Pct.drive.wkend +
  Avgdays.week +
  Brake.14miles +
  Right.turn.intensity12 +
  Left.turn.intensity12 +
  offset(log(Exposure))

m2_full <- glm.nb(
  formula = formula_glm2,
  data = train_glm
)
car::vif(m2_full)
# Modèle complet (M_1)
M_1 <- glm.nb(formula = formula_glm2,
  data = train_glm)
# Modèle réduit sans variable (M_0)
M_0 <- glm.nb(NB_Claim ~ 1, data = train_glm)

# Sélection stepwise basée sur AIC
model_aic2 <- stats :: step(M_0, 
                                scope = list(lower = M_0, upper = M_1),
                                direction = "both",
                                trace = 1)

summary(model_aic2)
drop1(model_aic2, test = "Chisq")
# we remove
# - Pct.drive.rush.pm
# - Right.turn.intensity12
model_aic2 <- update(
  model_aic2,
  . ~ . - c("Pct.drive.rush.pm", "Right.turn.intensity12") 
)
pseudo_r_2 = pR2(model_aic2)["McFadden"] # mcfarden pseudo r squard
```

- using vif, not too much multicolinearity issue in the dataset, all variables 
have vif < 3 
- second selection AIC based selction, then ANOVA 
## using validation test to compare both models 
```{r}
# generate validation predictions 
pred_aic1 <- predict(
  model_aic1,
  newdata = valid_glm,
  type = "response"
)

pred_aic2 <- predict(
  model_aic2,
  newdata = valid_glm,
  type = "response"
)
# Validation comparison function
compare_freq_model <- function(predictions,
                               observed,
                               exposure,
                               model_name,
                               theta = NULL) {

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((observed - predictions)^2))
  mae <- mean(abs(observed - predictions))
  observed_freq <- sum(observed) / sum(exposure)
  predicted_freq <- sum(predictions) / sum(exposure)
  calibration_error <- abs(
    observed_freq - predicted_freq
  )
  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,RMSE = rmse,MAE = mae, ObsFreq = observed_freq,
    PredFreq = predicted_freq,
    CalibrationError = calibration_error
  )
}
# compare models 
validation_results <- bind_rows(

  compare_freq_model(
    pred_aic1,
    valid_glm$NB_Claim,
    valid_glm$Exposure,
    "AIC Model 1"
  ),

  compare_freq_model(
    pred_aic2,
    valid_glm$NB_Claim,
    valid_glm$Exposure,
    "AIC Model 2"
  )

)

validation_results

# Compare Negative Binomial log-likelihood
ll_aic1 <- sum(
  dnbinom(
    valid_glm$NB_Claim,
    mu = pred_aic1,
    size = model_aic1$theta,
    log = TRUE
  )
)

ll_aic2 <- sum(
  dnbinom(
    valid_glm$NB_Claim,
    mu = pred_aic2,
    size = model_aic2$theta,
    log = TRUE
  )
)

data.frame(
  Model = c("AIC1", "AIC2"),
  ValidationLogLik = c(ll_aic1, ll_aic2)
)
# Visual comparison
errors_long <- validation_results %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -Model,
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

ggplot(
  errors_long,
  aes(Model, Value, fill = Metric)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Validation Set Comparison",
    x = "",
    y = ""
  )
```
- model 2 seemms to be slighty better , iw will check if the difference is stats signin
```{r}
ll1 <- dnbinom(
  valid_glm$NB_Claim,
  mu   = pred_aic1,
  size = model_aic1$theta,
  log  = TRUE
)

ll2 <- dnbinom(
  valid_glm$NB_Claim,
  mu   = pred_aic2,
  size = model_aic2$theta,
  log  = TRUE
)

# Paired t-test
t.test(ll1, ll2, paired = TRUE)
```

- the difference is statistically significant , so we keep model 2 

- now lasso ridge 
```{r}
library(glmnet)
# Design matrices for glmnet
x_train_mat <- model.matrix(~ ., data = X_train)[, -1]
x_valid_mat <- model.matrix(~ ., data = X_valid)[, -1]
x_test_mat  <- model.matrix(~ ., data = X_test)[, -1]

cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(
  x = x_train_mat,
  y = y_train,
  family = "poisson",
  alpha = 1,
  nfolds = 5,
  standardize = TRUE,
  offset = log(X_train$Exposure)
)
# Plot CV curve
plot(cv_lasso)
coef_lasso <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min")

selected_vars <- rownames(coef_lasso)[
  coef_lasso[, 1] != 0
]
# refitting using the selecting variables on a negative binomial 
selected_vars <- setdiff(selected_vars, c("(Intercept)"))

formula_nb <- as.formula(
  paste(
    "NB_Claim ~",
    paste(selected_vars, collapse = " + "), 
    "+ offset(log(Exposure))"
  )
)

# Refit Negative Binomial model
m_nb <- glm.nb(
  formula = formula_nb,
  data = train_glm
)

summary(m_nb)
AIC(m_nb)
```

# evaluation of models 
```{r}

# - m_nb : the one using lasso variables 
# - model_aic2 : the one using the bands
# - model_aic1 the one using the splines 

# Fonction pour calculer AUC et Gini

calculate_errors <- function(predictions, observed,
                             threshold = 0.5,
                             model_name) {
  
  pred_class <- factor(
    ifelse(predictions >= threshold, 1, 0),
    levels = c(0, 1)
  )
  
  actual_class <- factor(
    as.numeric(observed),
    levels = c(0, 1)
  )
  
  cm <- confusionMatrix(
    pred_class,
    actual_class,
    positive = "1"
  )
  
  roc_obj <- roc(actual_class, predictions, quiet = TRUE)
  auc_value <- as.numeric(auc(roc_obj))
  
  data.frame(
    Model       = model_name,
    Accuracy    = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    ErrorRate   = 1 - cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    Sensitivity = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    Precision   = cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
    F1_Score    = cm$byClass["F1"],
    AUC         = auc_value,
    Gini        = 2 * auc_value - 1,
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

errors <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  calculate_errors(pred_logit_selected, y_test, model_name = "Logit - Selected"),
  calculate_errors(pred_logit_lasso, y_test, model_name = "Logit - LASSO"),
  calculate_errors(pred_logit_combined, y_test, model_name = "logit - combined")
)

print(errors)

roc_combined <- roc(y_test, pred_logit_combined)

roc.test(roc_selected, roc_combined, method = "delong")
# p valuje being less than 1 % we confirm that the difference is stat signi
# so the he combined model significantly outperforms the selected model in AUC.
```

# 3. Modele CANN 
##  Architecture
The CANN blends a classical regression with a network by adding their linear predictors before the link:
- The log-linear part receives ONLY traditional risk factors. It is deliberately constrained — it provides the stable, interpretable backbone.

- The MLP receives traditional AND telematics inputs, so it can learn interactions BETWEEN them, not just telematics effects in isolation. This is exactly what the paper argues a manually engineered feature set cannot do.


```{r}
#separons les variables traditioneles et les telematrics 
trad_vars <- c(
  "Insured.age.band",
  "Car.age.band","Credit.score.band","Years.noclaims.band",
"Marital", "Region","Car.use.grp"
)

tele_vars <- c(
  "Total.miles.driven",
  "Pct.drive.rush.pm",
  "Pct.drive.rush.am",
  "Pct.drive.wkend",
  "Avgdays.week",
  "Brake.14miles",
  "Right.turn.intensity12",
  "Left.turn.intensity12"
)

# on récupère les coeffcients du modèle glm 
glm_base <- glm.nb(
  NB_Claim ~
    Insured.age.band +
    Car.age.band +
    Credit.score.band +
    Years.noclaims.band +
    Marital +
    Region +
    Car.use.grp +
    offset(log(Exposure)),
  data = train_glm
)
```
